subject: mathematics
question_text: If sin α = 1/√10, sin β = 1/√5 and α, β are acute, show that α + β = π/4.

mark_split.label: Find cos α and cos β
Find sin(α + β) and fix the quadrant

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 8 TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS, Very Short Answer question 25, book p.87. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1 + 1 gives one mark to the two cosines, where the acute condition decides the sign of the square root, and one to the addition formulas — including the cos(α + β) check, without which 3π/4 is not ruled out. Paper position: Maths-1A Section A prints ten very short answers of 2 marks each and the student writes all ten, under the 2026-27 pattern; Trigonometric Ratios and Transformations supplies two of those ten slots. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would show this — name what you find first, and how you decide between π/4 and 3π/4.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Find cos α and cos β
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both angles are acute, so both cosines are positive and the positive square root is the right one. cos α = 3/√10 and cos β = 2/√5.
steps.memory_tip: Acute means the cosine is positive, so take the plus sign on both square roots.
lines: α and β are acute, so cos α > 0, cos β > 0

recall.must_convey: That cos α = 3/√10 and cos β = 2/√5, with the positive root taken because both angles are acute.
accept: use sin squared plus cos squared equals one to get the cosines
cos alpha is three by root ten and cos beta is two by root five
both are acute so the cosines are positive
acute kabatti cosine positive, plus root teeskovali
take the positive square root for both

steps.why: Both cosines are needed for the addition formula, and only the word acute tells you which sign of the square root to take. A negative cosine would put the sum in a different quadrant and the proof would fail.
common_mistakes: Taking the negative square root for a cosine.
Using 1 + sin²θ in place of 1 − sin²θ.

steps.label: Find sin(α + β) and fix the quadrant
steps.margin_note: Second mark. sin(α + β) = 1/√2 alone allows π/4 and 3π/4. cos(α + β) = 1/√2 is positive, which leaves only π/4.
steps.memory_tip: Sine alone leaves two answers, π/4 and 3π/4. The sign of the cosine decides which one.
lines: sin(α + β) = sinα cosβ + cosα sinβ
cos(α + β) = cosα cosβ − sinα sinβ
Both α and β are acute, so 0 < α + β < π,

recall.must_convey: That sin(α + β) = 1/√2, that cos(α + β) = 1/√2 is positive, and that this rules out 3π/4 and leaves π/4.
accept: sin of alpha plus beta is one by root two
also find cos of alpha plus beta and it is positive so the sum is in the first quadrant
sine alone gives pi by four or three pi by four so check the cosine
cos kuda positive kabatti pi by four matrame
the sum is forty five degrees
reject: cos alpha is three by root ten

steps.why: sin(α + β) = 1/√2 is satisfied by π/4 and by 3π/4, so the sine alone does not finish the proof. Cosine separates them: it is positive at π/4 and negative at 3π/4, so showing cos(α + β) > 0 is what makes the answer unique.
common_mistakes: Stopping at sin(α + β) = 1/√2 and writing π/4 without ruling out 3π/4.
A sign slip in cos(α + β) = cosα cosβ − sinα sinβ.
